claims.text: Crystal-structure selection in noble-metal high-entropy alloy nanoparticles containing more than five elements is governed by kinetic trapping during rapid thermal processing.
Very short high-temperature exposure promotes rapid, approximately simultaneous decomposition of mixed metal precursors into a homogenized liquid or quasi-liquid state.
Rapid cooling freezes the homogenized multimetal state into a single-phase disordered solid solution.
A modest extension of high-temperature dwell time provides enough atomic mobility for enthalpically driven segregation.
Dwell-time-induced segregation will produce phase separation and non-uniform elemental distributions.
The starting material is a mixture of noble-metal precursors intended to produce a nanoparticle containing more than five elements.
The controlled intervention is to increase the high-temperature dwell time after precursor decomposition and before rapid cooling.
The baseline process heats precursor-loaded carbon or a similar inert support within tens of milliseconds and then cools it rapidly.
The intervention can use a dwell of several seconds while holding all other synthesis parameters fixed.
Precursor decomposition produces or nucleates a quasi-liquid multimetal droplet.
Extremely short exposure and rapid cooling limit atomic diffusion and thereby suppress segregation and phase separation.
With greater high-temperature mobility, local diffusion follows preferences associated with pairwise mixing enthalpies.
An extended dwell causes uncontrolled particle growth.
Relative to rapid flash heating, an extended dwell will increase elemental segregation and secondary-phase formation.
Relative to the baseline, an extended dwell will make particle morphology less uniform.
Rapid flash heating for tens of milliseconds followed by immediate cooling provides the single-phase, uniformly alloyed baseline.

The proposed mechanism applies to noble-metal systems with more than five elements when the peak temperature melts or decomposes all precursors and cooling remains fast enough to trap metastable configurations.
The segregation-onset dwell time is unquantified and may vary with elemental combination and precursor loading.
No significant dwell-dependent change in phase homogeneity, elemental distribution, or morphology would falsify the kinetic-trapping hypothesis.
